notes: Ruling slot 0 = PSD (Bourguiba; Bahi Ladgham PM since Nov 1969). Coalition slot 13 has no separate party in the single-party system, so it holds the presidential court around Wassila Bourguiba. Mestiri's liberal Destourians in 2 (popularity slot; MD's later MDS sits in 3), UGTT in 3 (ICFTU member). Perspectives/GEAST in 19 as precursor of MD's Workers' Party; student left in 5. Youssefists as anti-Western pan-Arab conservatives in 6, Ba'ath in 7. No Shia in 1970 Tunisia: slot 8 = taqrib circle, slot 9 = Djerba Ibadis (imamate doctrine).

0.name: al-Hizb al-Ishtiraki al-Dusturi
0.text:
The Socialist Destourian Party is the sole legal party of Tunisia, heir to the Neo-Destour that Habib Bourguiba founded at Ksar Hellal in 1934 and renamed at the Bizerte congress of 1964. On 1 January 1970 it is shaking off a collectivist decade: Ahmed Ben Salah was dismissed in September 1969 and Bahi Ladgham now heads the government as prime minister.

The party embodies Bourguibism: a secular, modernizing presidential state, the Personal Status Code, mass education and a firmly pro-Western foreign policy that keeps Nasser and the Soviet bloc at arm's length. Its leverage lies in a dense network of branches, the national organizations it controls and the towering authority of the Supreme Combatant.

1.name: Les Hommes de la Banque centrale
1.native_full: Les Hommes de la Banque centrale
1.text:
The Central Bank men are the circle of financial technocrats gathered around Hedi Nouira, a founding figure of the Neo-Destour who has governed the Central Bank of Tunisia since its creation in 1958. Sceptical of Ben Salah's cooperatives from the start, they are emerging from the wreckage of the collectivist experiment as the obvious architects of a new course.

They favour sound money, private initiative, foreign investment and close economic ties with France, the European Community and the United States, while keeping the single party and the strong presidency intact. Their leverage lies in their control of credit and the budget, their standing with Western lenders and Bourguiba's growing trust.

2.name: Les Libéraux destouriens
2.text:
The Destourian liberals are the reform wing of the ruling party, led by Ahmed Mestiri, who left the cabinet in 1968 in protest against Ben Salah's collectivism and the absence of debate inside the party. Around him gather ministers, diplomats and lawyers of the Neo-Destour generation who see the fall of Ben Salah as proof that one-man rule produces disasters.

They call for internal party democracy, elected rather than appointed leaderships, freedom of the press and a genuine separation of powers, all within a firmly pro-Western Tunisia. Their base is the educated Tunis bourgeoisie, younger cadres and part of the party's middle ranks, and their leverage rests on their credibility at the next party congress.

3.name: al-Ittihad al-'Amm al-Tunisi li-l-Shughl
3.text:
The Tunisian General Labour Union is the country's only trade union centre, founded in 1946 by Farhat Hached, whose assassination in 1952 made him a national martyr. It fought for independence alongside the Neo-Destour, but Bourguiba has repeatedly brought it to heel, removing its leader Habib Achour in 1965; with Ben Salah gone, Achour is regaining influence over the union.

A member of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, it stands for collective bargaining, wage rises, social security and a democratic socialism of the Western European kind rather than state collectivism. Its leverage lies in its hold over the phosphate mines, the docks, the railways and public services, and in its ability to call general strikes.

4.name: al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Tunisi
4.text:
The Tunisian Communist Party grew out of the French Communist Party's Tunisian federation and became autonomous in 1934. It has been banned since January 1963, after the authorities linked it to the failed coup plot of December 1962. Under its first secretary Mohamed Ennafaa it survives as a small, disciplined and semi-clandestine organization of intellectuals, teachers and trade unionists.

Loyal to Moscow, it denounces Tunisia's alignment with the United States and France and calls for the legalization of political parties, land reform, a planned economy and friendship with the socialist camp. Its leverage lies in its influence among students and in some union sections, and in the goodwill of the Soviet Union.

5.name: La Gauche estudiantine
5.text:
The student left is the radical milieu that has made the University of Tunis the main arena of opposition since the riots of June 1967 and the strikes of March 1968. Its rallying cause is Mohamed Ben Jennet, a theology student sentenced to twenty years' hard labour after the pro-Arab demonstrations of June 1967, together with the activists jailed alongside the Perspectives group.

It rejects the ruling party's control of the General Union of Tunisian Students, demands academic freedom and an amnesty, and mixes Marxism, Arab nationalism and solidarity with the Palestinian fedayeen and Vietnam. Its strength lies in faculties and lycées, in its capacity to paralyse the campus and in a generation that no longer reveres the founders of the state.

6.name: al-Yusufiyyun
6.text:
The Youssefists are the followers of Salah Ben Youssef, Bourguiba's great rival, who rejected the 1955 autonomy conventions, led the Neo-Destour's General Secretariat into revolt with Cairo's backing and was assassinated in Frankfurt in 1961. Hunted down by the state, the movement survives through exiles in Cairo and Algiers, veterans of the armed bands and a scattering of Zitouna-educated sympathizers.

It condemns Bourguiba as a servant of France and the West and wants Tunisia anchored in the Arab and Islamic world at Nasser's side, with Arabic restored as the language of the state and religion respected. Its leverage lies in the south, Djerba and the Zitouna milieu, and in the revolutionary regimes now flanking Tunisia in Tripoli and Algiers.

7.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki - Qutr Tunis
7.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Tunisia Region
7.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki - Qutr Tunis
7.text:
The Tunisian branch of the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party is a clandestine network of teachers, students and graduates of Damascus and Baghdad universities, repeatedly broken up by Bourguiba's police. Since the 1966 schism in the Ba'ath its members are divided between loyalty to Damascus and to Baghdad, and it has no public leaders.

It preaches unity, freedom and socialism: one Arab nation from the Gulf to the Atlantic, a revolutionary single party, nationalization and an end to Tunisia's Western orientation in favour of the anti-imperialist Arab camp and Soviet arms. Its leverage lies in classrooms and Arabic-language schools and among young Tunisians who see Damascus, Baghdad and now Tripoli as models.

8.name: Ahl al-Taqrib
8.text:
Ahl al-Taqrib is a small circle of Zitouna-trained teachers and preachers drawn to the movement for rapprochement between the Islamic schools, launched in Cairo in 1947 with the support of al-Azhar and Shia scholars from Iran and Iraq. They read Shia reformist authors, follow the writings coming out of Najaf and cherish the Fatimid heritage of Mahdia.

They argue that the divide between Sunni and Shia is a political wound inflicted by tyrants, and that a reformed Islam of justice and love for the Prophet's family can rally the poor against a secular, Westernized state. Their audience is tiny, confined to a few mosques and study circles in Tunis and the Sahel, but their ideas could find fertile ground among disillusioned students.

9.name: Ibadiyyu Jarba
9.text:
The Ibadis of Djerba are the last stronghold in Tunisia of the Ibadi school, a branch of Islam neither Sunni nor Shia that once ruled much of the Maghreb through elected imams. Their mosques, Koranic schools and councils of learned sheikhs still regulate the religious and family life of the island's Berber-speaking villages and of the Djerbian merchant community in Tunis and France.

Their doctrine holds that the community must be led by a just imam chosen by the learned and deposed if he strays, and that the scholars stand above any ruler in moral authority. Wary of Bourguiba's secular reforms, they are disciplined, prosperous through commerce and tightly organized, a living model of clerical self-government.

10.name: 'Ulama' al-Zaytuna
10.text:
The Zitouna ulama are the scholars of the ancient Zitouna mosque-university, for centuries the guardians of Maliki law and of the beylical state's religious offices. Bourguiba stripped them of the sharia courts, the habous endowments and their autonomous university, which became a faculty of theology in 1961; Sheikh Mohamed Tahar Ben Achour, the most eminent of them, embodies both their dignity and their defeat.

They are not revolutionaries: they seek to restore Islamic education, the status of Arabic and religious law in family matters within the existing order, and they welcome any ruler who honours the faith. Their influence survives in the mosques, among traditional families of Tunis and the interior and in a public offended by the 1960 campaign against the Ramadan fast.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Sheikh Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, has begun to win its first Tunisian adherents among students and teachers who studied in the Mashriq. Its Tunisian presence is a handful of discreet study circles without public leaders, operating under the eyes of a police that treats every religious network as subversive.

The party rejects nationalism, the republic and democracy alike and calls for the restoration of the caliphate, which it expects to achieve by winning over army officers rather than through elections or mass action. Its leverage is small but patient: an elaborate doctrine, strict secrecy and a cell structure designed to survive repression.

12.name: al-Jama'a al-Islamiyya
12.text:
The Islamic Group is the nucleus of a new Islamist movement taking shape around Rached Ghannouchi, a philosophy graduate who returned from Damascus and Paris in 1969, and the young Tunis preacher Abdelfattah Mourou. Through sermons, mosque lessons and informal meetings, they are gathering a following of high-school and university students alarmed by the secular course of Bourguiba's republic.

Inspired by the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, they call for the re-Islamization of society, the defence of Arabic and public morality and a return to Islam as a complete way of life, rejecting both Western liberalism and Marxism. For now they avoid confronting the state and rely on preaching and personal networks.

13.name: Le Sérail
13.text:
Le Sérail is the presidential court that has formed around the ageing and often ailing Habib Bourguiba, with his wife Wassila Ben Ammar at its centre. Ministers, governors and businessmen owe their careers to her favour, she was among those who turned the president against Ben Salah in 1969, and she keeps her own channels to Arab capitals and to Paris.

The court has no ideology beyond preserving Bourguiba's rule and managing his succession. It prizes stability, patronage and a balanced foreign policy free of bloc commitments, and favours pragmatic deals with Gulf money and Arab neighbours. Its leverage lies in its control of access to the president, of appointments and of the timing of every political decision.

14.name: Union nationale des agriculteurs tunisiens
14.text:
The National Union of Tunisian Farmers is the organization of the country's landowning farmers, from the olive growers of the Sahel and Sfax to the cereal estates of the north. Integrated into the Destourian system as one of its national organizations, it was humiliated in 1969 when Ben Salah sought to fold all private land into cooperatives, a drive that provoked riots in the Sahel and was abandoned in September.

It stands for private property, fair producer prices, rural credit and the return of land taken during the cooperative campaign, and it distrusts both the left and the urban bureaucracy. Its leverage lies in rural notables, the olive and grain economy and the president's need to win back the countryside.

15.name: Union tunisienne de l'industrie, du commerce et de l'artisanat
15.english: Tunisian Confederation of Industry, Trade and Handicrafts
15.native_full: Union tunisienne de l'industrie, du commerce et de l'artisanat
15.text:
The Tunisian Confederation of Industry, Trade and Handicrafts is the employers' organization of Tunisia, founded in 1947 and since independence one of the national organizations allied to the ruling party. Led by Ferjani Bel Hadj Ammar, it speaks for industrialists, wholesalers, contractors and the old commercial families of Tunis and Sfax, many of whom saw their trade swallowed by state cooperatives in 1969.

It wants the private sector restored, credit opened to entrepreneurs, tax relief, protection against foreign competition where needed and open doors to European investment and tourism. Its leverage lies in its role in wage bargaining with the UGTT, in its members' wealth and in their proximity to the technocrats now taking charge of the economy.
15.wiki: Tunisian Confederation of Industry, Trade and Handicrafts

16.name: Les Commerçants de la Médina
16.text:
The merchants of the Medina are the shopkeepers, wholesalers and artisans of the souks of Tunis, Sfax and Sousse, together with the grocers from Djerba and the south who run small shops across the country. In 1969 they were the last victims of Ben Salah's experiment, when retail trade was to be absorbed into state cooperatives; his fall has left them vindicated and determined never to be expropriated again.

They want free trade, low taxes, an end to price controls and licences, and a state that leaves the market alone. Politically cautious and pious, they have no party of their own but finance whoever protects property. Their leverage lies in their control of retail distribution, their savings and networks reaching into every town.

17.name: Les Gardiens des Oasis
17.text:
The Guardians of the Oases are the palm-grove farmers, water engineers and agronomists of the Djerid and Nefzaoua who are sounding the alarm over the fate of Tunisia's southern oases. New deep wells, salinization and the advance of the dunes threaten springs and gardens that have sustained the south for millennia, while in the north the forests are lost to grazing and charcoal burning.

They call for protecting water tables and springs, reforestation, the fight against desertification and respect for traditional water-sharing rules, rather than prestige projects decided in Tunis. They have no party and no national leader, but they speak for the rural south, the foresters and the scientists of the agricultural institutes.

18.name: Les Coopérativistes
18.text:
The cooperativists are the planners, cadres and true believers of the cooperative experiment that Ahmed Ben Salah drove through as minister of planning and finance from 1961. Dismissed in September 1969 and disowned by the party, Ben Salah now faces prosecution as the scapegoat for the crisis, while his followers in the ministries, the cooperatives and the unions are being purged.

They defend Destourian socialism as adopted at the Bizerte congress of 1964: central planning, collective land and production units and state-led industrialization to lift the poor regions. Non-aligned and drawn to Scandinavian and Yugoslav models, they still command loyalty among agronomists, young cadres and landless peasants who gained work through the cooperatives.

19.name: Groupe d'études et d'action socialiste tunisien
19.english: Tunisian Socialist Study and Action Group
19.native_full: Groupe d'études et d'action socialiste tunisien
19.text:
The Tunisian Socialist Study and Action Group, known by its review Perspectives tunisiennes, was founded by Tunisian students in Paris in 1963 and became the backbone of the new left at home. Its leaders, including Gilbert Naccache, Ahmed Ben Othman and Noureddine Ben Khader, were sentenced to long prison terms in 1968, yet the group survives underground and is turning to Maoism through its Arabic-language paper El Amel Ettounsi.

It rejects both the Destourian regime and the pro-Soviet communists, calls for a people's democratic revolution led by workers and peasants, and draws inspiration from China, Vietnam and the Palestinian resistance. Its base is the university, the lycées and a growing circle of young teachers and workers.

20.name: Les Fellaghas
20.text:
The fellaghas are the veterans of the armed bands that fought the French in the mountains and the south between 1952 and 1954, together with the families of the resistance martyrs. Many feel cheated by an independence that brought the lawyers and notables of the Sahel to power while former fighters were disarmed, ignored or, if they sided with Ben Youssef, hunted down; the conspiracy of December 1962 drew several of them in.

They cultivate a fierce, plebeian nationalism: suspicion of France and its interests, contempt for the Francophone elite, demands for pensions, land and jobs for those who bled for the nation, and a cult of the strong patriotic leader. Their leverage lies in the poor interior and among veterans' associations.

21.name: Les Milices destouriennes
21.text:
The Destourian militias are the ruling party's strong-arm squads, heirs of the vigilance committees that the Neo-Destour turned against the Youssefists in 1955 and 1956, when rivals were beaten, kidnapped or killed. Their men are recruited among party toughs, Destourian youth and the unemployed of the popular quarters, and they answer to the party apparatus rather than to the law.

They stand for the cult of the Supreme Combatant, the fusion of nation, party and leader, and the physical suppression of opponents, from Youssefists and communists to striking workers and students. They despise parliamentary debate and see the liberals as traitors. Their leverage lies in the party's local cells and the ease with which the regime can mobilize them in a crisis.

22.name: al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Tunisiyya
22.text:
The Tunisian Armed Forces were created in 1956 from Tunisian units of the French and beylical armies and remain deliberately small. Bourguiba keeps them out of politics, entrusts the defence ministry to civilians and has watched the officer corps closely since the abortive conspiracy of December 1962; Béji Caïd Essebsi currently heads the Defence Ministry.

Trained and equipped mainly by France and the United States, the officers are professional, pro-Western and wary of the Algerian and Libyan revolutions on their borders. They would intervene only to preserve order or secure the succession. Their leverage lies in their monopoly of force, the memory of Bizerte in 1961 and the prestige of an institution comparatively insulated from party patronage.

23.name: al-Usra al-Husayniyya
23.text:
The Husainid dynasty ruled Tunisia as beys from 1705 until Bourguiba deposed Muhammad VIII al-Amin and proclaimed the republic on 25 July 1957. The last bey died in 1962 after years of humiliation, and the princes of the house live quietly in Tunis and abroad, stripped of their palaces and property and watched by the authorities.

Monarchism has no organization in Tunisia, but nostalgia for the beylical order survives among old Tunis families, former palace retainers and religious notables who resented the abolition of their privileges. They imagine a constitutional monarchy that would reconcile Islamic legitimacy with modern government, a vision that only a collapse of Bourguibism could revive.
